tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: send_message_to_user_async
tools.description: Send a concise message that needs the user's attention during ongoing work. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Use this tool to report a critical blocker or a finding that may change the task's direction, or to answer a user question or status request received while work is still in progress. Use this tool when a message needs the user's immediate attention; use commentary for routine progress and intermediate context. Use clear formatting, such as bolding questions, to make requests easy to notice and answer.

message.description: The concise question or update to send to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-terra`: Legacy balanced model for agentic coding. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-luna`: Legacy fast model for simpler tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.5`: Legacy coding model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

tools.name: mcp__cua_repl
tools.description: UI automation through cua_repl using the initialized cua API.

tools.name: js
tools.description:
Control native apps or browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built skills, connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.

On the first invocation of `cua_repl`, or after resetting it, execute exactly one of the API calls shown below, optionally assigning its result to a variable. Do not add other API calls, waits, or snapshots to that invocation.
The tool result will include documentation and, when creating or selecting a tab or selecting an app, its initial UI state. Selecting a browser does not open a tab. Read that result before continuing.
Use only APIs described in the tool instructions or returned documentation.

When you need an inventory of available apps, browsers, and tabs, get a snapshot of all enabled surfaces. Otherwise, use the relevant entry point below:

```javascript
await cua.getState();
```

Use the first matching browser control option from the user's request:

For a tab @-mention (`mention=tab-v1`):
Pass the complete `plugin://...` URL to get the referenced tab.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ mention: tabMentionUrl });
```

For an existing tab identified by URL in browser context (including the current IAB tab):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ url }, { browser: browserId });
```

Known tab ID (`tabId` or `providerTabId`) and browser (name or browser @-mention):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: browserId });
```

To open a URL in the in-app browser (`@Browser`):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", url, { visible: boolean });
```

To open a URL in another named browser: pass its name directly; do not call `getBrowser` first.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(browserName, url, browserOptions);
```

Known URL, only when the user has not specified a browser by name or @-mention:

```javascript
let browser = await cua.getBrowser({ url });
```

Browser IDs and options:

- `"mcpapps"`: use `cua.getBrowser({ id: "mcpapps" })` for existing full-screen MCP Apps in the task’s side panel.
- `"iab"` (in-app browser): in `createBrowserTab`, use `visible: true` to show the browser; `false` to keep it hidden.
- `"dot"` (Dot): use only when present in browser inventory. It accesses tabs on Dot's active main thread. `cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: "dot" })` selects an existing tab. `cua.createBrowserTab("dot", url, { visible: boolean })` creates one with the same visibility options as `"iab"`.
- `"chrome"` (@Chrome), `"edge"` (@Edge): pass a short, emoji-prefixed `sessionName` (e.g. `"🔎 Task"`) to `createBrowserTab` when starting a task.

If the user specifies an app to use, get the app by name, bundle ID, or path:

```javascript
let app = await cua.getApp("Example App");
```

To add other content to the tool result, use `nodeRepl.write(value)` for text or other values and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(image)` for images. The APIs listed above already display their documentation or UI state; do not wrap their results in `write` or `emitImage`.

If your context begins with a summary of an existing computer use task, call `await cua.rewriteDocumentation()` before continuing the computer use task to ensure you have a complete view of the necessary documentation.

Each `cua_repl.js` call opens or continues a browser activity. Keep consecutive calls together. The activity stays open across messages until you emit completion commentary.

**Manual takeover takes priority over the table below.** For a required manual browser step, call the documented takeover API before asking the user to act, unless takeover is already pending. Explain the required step in your final reply. Tab marking alone does not transfer control. While waiting for the user to finish and return control, emit no completion and make no CUA calls, even when answering side questions. The takeover API returning does not end this wait. When the user returns or unblocks you, resume browser work and apply the table. If they cancel, replace, or no longer need the browser work, close the activity before answering, even without another CUA call.

Completion is a standalone assistant commentary message containing only `::browser-complete{title="<headline>"}`. Never put it in a tool call or final reply. Use 3–6 words starting with a past-tense verb to describe the observed outcome. Omit identifiers.

After a user cancels pending browser work: commentary `::browser-complete{title="Stopped browser work"}`, then the final acknowledgement. No browser call is needed.

For an open browser activity:

| Next action                                   | Required output order                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Another CUA call                              | Continue without completion.                                                              |
| A non-CUA tool, final reply, or chat question | Finish required tab marking, emit completion, then take that action in the same response. |

With no open activity, emit no completion. Later CUA use requires a fresh completion at the next table boundary.

If you need a one-time sign-in code, information, or confirmation from the user, follow the table and ask in chat. One-time code entry alone does not require takeover. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

code.description: JavaScript to execute using the initialized cua_repl runtime.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Prefer a few words in present-progressive form, such as 'Checking the mobile layout' or 'Comparing prices', over imperative or past-tense titles.

tools.name: js_reset
tools.description: Reset the persistent cua_repl JavaScript session. All JavaScript bindings are discarded. The next cua_repl.js call initializes a fresh runtime for the enabled surfaces. This does not close browser tabs or native apps, or erase their state. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/alexcallow/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/egm/egm/0.1.1/skills`
- `r3` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: API first-timers, Codex/Work Q&A. If the user already has an OpenAI API integration, skip this skill for API questions and use the developer docs. Read this skill before answering how Codex or ChatGPT Work behaves, where to find a feature, or how to configure or troubleshoot this app or coding agent. This includes conversation history, model and cache behavior, instruction precedence, permissions, and tool availability. Use for API onboarding only when the user is connecting to the OpenAI API for the first time. Skip action requests, such as scheduling an automation, and tasks fully answered by supplied text or data. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- apollo-client: Guide for building React applications with Apollo Client 4.x. Use this skill when: (1) setting up Apollo Client in a React project, (2) writing GraphQL queries or mutations with hooks, (3) configuring caching or cache policies, (4) managing local state with reactive variables, (5) troubleshooting Apollo Client errors or performance issues. (file: r0/apollo-client/SKILL.md)
- built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Codex desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Codex's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It is not for Codex in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (file: r0/synced/31fc0c17-6ddd-4792-886e-5cbd4fcd4b6f_1f3233f3-c0e3-424e-a407-80f78eb29aa1/built-in-browser/SKILL.md)
- chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Codex in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. - code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/PRD asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X". (file: r0/code-review/SKILL.md)

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"

## When to request escalation

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Suggested infrastructure for the Frame Inventory exercise.
#
# This compose file is a starting point, not a requirement. You are free to
# swap any of these services for tooling you prefer (a different database,
# search engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final
# stack still runs end-to-end with a single command.
#
# If you do choose to use the services provided here, pick ONE of the two
# datastores for your domain data — either `mongodb` or `postgres`,
# not both. Remove the service you do not need (and its volume) so the
# stack reflects the design you actually built.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

services:
  backend:
    build:
      context: ./src/backend
    container_name: frame-inventory-backend
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4000:4000"
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
      - "127.0.0.1:9090:9090"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:+,local-import}
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/frames
      SPRING_FLYWAY_ENABLED: "true"
      MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE: health,info,prometheus
      SENTRY_DSN: ${SENTRY_DSN:-}
      SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: ${SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT:-local}
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN: ${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:-}
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_BUCKET: frame-inventory-import-local
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_REGION: us-east-1
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_SIGNING_ENDPOINT: http://127.0.0.1:4566
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_ENABLED: "true"
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_AWS_ENDPOINT: http://aws:4566
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_QUEUE_URL: http://aws:4566/000000000000/inventory-import
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_DLQ_URL: http://aws:4566/000000000000/inventory-import-dlq
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_TARGET: temporal:7233
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: test
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: test
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      aws:
        condition: service_healthy
      temporal:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator/health"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      frame-inventory:
        aliases: [bff]

  bff:
    build:
      context: ./src
      dockerfile: bff/Dockerfile
    # Keep the import gRPC connection on loopback.
    network_mode: service:backend
    environment:
      FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT: ${FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT:-127.0.0.1:9090}
      IMPORT_GRPC_ENDPOINT: ${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:+127.0.0.1:9090}
      BFF_LISTEN_HOST: 0.0.0.0
      OTEL_EXPORTER_PROMETHEUS_HOST: 0.0.0.0
      SENTRY_DSN: ${BFF_SENTRY_DSN:-}
      SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: ${SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT:-local}
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy

  frontend:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: src/frontend/Dockerfile
    container_name: frame-inventory-frontend
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    environment:
      BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8080
      BFF_URL: http://bff:4000
    volumes:
      - ./src/frontend/src:/app/src/frontend/src
      - ./src/frontend/public:/app/src/frontend/public
      - ./src/frontend/next.config.ts:/app/src/frontend/next.config.ts:ro
      - ./design-system:/app/design-system:ro
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - bff
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  aws:
    image: localstack/localstack:4.12.0
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4566:4566"
    environment:
      SERVICES: s3,sqs
      AWS_DEFAULT_REGION: us-east-1
      SQS_ENDPOINT_STRATEGY: dynamic
      S3_SKIP_SIGNATURE_VALIDATION: "0"
    volumes:
      - ./infra/inventory-import/local/init-aws.sh:/etc/localstack/init/ready.d/init-aws.sh:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "test", "-f", "/tmp/inventory-import-ready"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  temporal:
    image: temporalio/temporal:1.5.1
    command: ["server", "start-dev", "--ip", "0.0.0.0"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:7233:7233"
      - "127.0.0.1:8233:8233"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "temporal", "operator", "cluster", "health", "--address", "127.0.0.1:7233"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  workflows:
    build:
      context: ./src
      dockerfile: workflows/Dockerfile
    network_mode: service:backend
    environment:
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN: ${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:-}
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_TARGET: temporal:7233
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy
    stop_grace_period: 25s

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18.6
    container_name: frame-inventory-postgres
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: frames
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 15
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.16.0
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:9091:9090"
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - bff
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  otel-collector:
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.165.0
    command: ["--config=/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:9464:9464"
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/otel-collector.yml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml:ro
    depends_on:
      - backend
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  loki:
    image: grafana/loki:3.7.0
    command: ["-config.file=/etc/loki/frame-inventory.yml"]
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/loki.yml:/etc/loki/frame-inventory.yml:ro
      - loki-data:/loki
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  alloy:
    image: grafana/alloy:v1.21.0
    command: ["run", "--storage.path=/var/lib/alloy/data", "/etc/alloy/config.alloy"]
    environment:
      COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME: ${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME}
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/config.alloy:/etc/alloy/config.alloy:ro
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - alloy-data:/var/lib/alloy/data
    depends_on:
      - loki
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:13.3.2
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3001:3000"
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/grafana-datasource.yml:/etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yml:ro
      - ./monitoring/grafana-dashboard-provider.yml:/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/frame-inventory.yml:ro
      - ./monitoring/dashboards:/etc/grafana/dashboards:ro
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
    depends_on:
      - prometheus
      - alloy
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  prometheus-data:
  grafana-data:
  loki-data:
  alloy-data:

networks:
  frame-inventory:
    driver: bridge
services:
  prometheus:
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/prometheus-local-import.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
# Frame Inventory

Application for the frame-inventory take-home exercise.

## System Overview

Next.js serves the inventory and import workspace. It sends GraphQL requests through a same-origin route to the BFF, which calls Spring Boot over gRPC. Docker Compose runs these services alongside PostgreSQL, Temporal, a local S3/SQS emulator, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and the OpenTelemetry Collector. The exercise provides a legacy export in `data/inventory_frame.csv` and describes the inventory features in `INSTRUCTIONS.md`.

Bring the whole stack up with one command.

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

Once PostgreSQL is healthy, the backend applies pending Flyway migrations during startup.

If you have `just` installed, run `just` to list the available recipes.

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `just up` | Build and start the whole stack in the foreground. |
| `just down` | Stop the stack and retain its named data volumes. |
| `just compose logs -f backend` | Pass arguments through to Docker Compose. |
| `just migrate` | Run Flyway on its own in a one-off backend container. |

## Subdirectories & System Boundaries

- [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the Spring Boot backend, Apollo Server BFF, and Next.js frontend.
- [Design system](./design-system/README.md) contains the prototype, sample frame data, and visual conventions for the exercise.

## Services

`docker compose up` starts the following services.

| Service               | Host port | Container port | Notes                                                  |
|-----------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| frontend              | 3000      | 3000           | Next.js workspace and same-origin GraphQL route     |
| bff                   | 4000      | 4000           | Apollo Sandbox and the frame inventory GraphQL API     |
| backend               | 8080      | 8080           | Spring Boot, exposes `GET /api/health`                 |
| postgres              | 5432      | 5432           | Spring Boot applies the inventory schema via Flyway    |
| aws                   | 4566      | 4566           | Local S3 and SQS for CSV imports                      |
| temporal              | 7233, 8233 | 7233, 8233    | Temporal gRPC and web UI                              |
| workflows             |           |              | Python Temporal worker for DELTA imports              |
| prometheus            | 9091      | 9090           | Scrapes Spring Boot and Apollo metrics every 15 seconds |
| otel-collector        | 9464      | 9464           | Scrapes Spring Boot metrics for local inspection       |
| grafana               | 3001      | 3000           | Queries provisioned Prometheus and Loki data            |

### Credentials

| Service               | User       | Password       | Database         |
|-----------------------|------------|----------------|------------------|
| postgres              | `app`      | `app`          | `frames`         |
| grafana               | `admin`    | `admin`         | n/a              |

## Global Invariants

- The Next.js rewrite preserves the `/api/` path and uses `BACKEND_URL` as its destination origin. Compose sets it to `http://backend:8080`. `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.frontend.environment.BACKEND_URL]`
- The Next.js `/api/graphql` route proxies GraphQL to `BFF_URL`. Compose sets it to `http://bff:4000`.

## Global Side Effects

- Opening the frontend loads the first page of frames. Starting an import uploads the file directly to S3 using the signed URL returned by the BFF.
- Docker Compose publishes service ports and creates named volumes for PostgreSQL, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and Alloy. `[docker-compose.yml:services]` `[docker-compose.yml:volumes]`

## System Verification

- From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test`.
- From `src/frontend`, run `npm run lint` after installing dependencies.

### Git hooks

Install [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/#installation), then run `pre-commit install`
from the repository root to install both Git hooks. The `pre-commit` hook checks
YAML, JSON, and merge conflict markers, and runs ESLint when staged changes touch
`src/frontend/`. Install the frontend dependencies with `npm ci --prefix src/frontend`
before committing frontend changes.

The `commit-msg` hook uses Commitlint to enforce the Conventional Commits format
documented in [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md). Commitlint requires Node.js 22.12 or newer.

Run `pre-commit run --all-files` to check the whole repository.

### Smoke test

Once the stack is up, check the service entry points.

- Open <http://localhost:3000> to view the frame list. See the [frontend setup](./src/frontend/README.md) to enable local imports.
- Hit the backend directly: <http://localhost:8080/api/health>.
- Open [Apollo Sandbox](http://127.0.0.1:4000) and run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md).

### Backend metrics

- Open [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets) and wait for the
  `frame-inventory-backend` target to show **UP**. It scrapes
  `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus` on the Compose network.
- Open [Grafana](http://127.0.0.1:3001), sign in with the initial credentials
  above, and run `up{job="frame-inventory-backend"}` in **Explore** using the
  default Prometheus data source. A value of `1` confirms the backend is being scraped.
- Open [Frame Inventory Backend](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-backend/frame-inventory-backend)
  for HTTP and gRPC request rate, errors, p50, p95, and p99 latency, and resource saturation.
  Generate API traffic and allow at least two Prometheus scrapes for request graphs
  to populate.
- The **Frame inventory activity** section shows committed creates, updates, and
  soft deletes, plus successful gRPC reads and version conflicts. The totals cover
  the dashboard time range. Rejected or rolled-back writes and repeated deletes
  that change no data are excluded from the totals.

Prometheus and Grafana listen on localhost. Their named volumes keep metrics
and Grafana settings across restarts.

### DELTA import dashboard

The main Compose stack scrapes import metrics from the backend. For the
host-based [local import setup](src/backend/README.md#local-import-operator),
start Spring Boot with the dispatcher enabled and run the
[Python worker](src/workflows/README.md). Set
`MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE=health,info,prometheus` and keep HTTP
port 8080 reachable from Docker. On Docker Desktop, scrape that host backend
with the local import Compose override.

```sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f monitoring/compose.local-import.yml \
  up -d --no-deps prometheus grafana
```

Open [Frame Inventory Imports](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-imports/frame-inventory-imports)
to see the oldest pending and running jobs, terminal dispatch failures in the
last hour, and mean and p95 apply duration. The age uses dispatch confirmation
when available and job creation otherwise. Apply duration covers each activity
attempt, including retries. Use the import job ID to find its
`csv-import-<jobId>` workflow when investigating a specific job.

To return to scraping the containerized backend and BFF, run
`docker compose up -d prometheus grafana` with the standard Compose configuration.

### BFF metrics

Run `docker compose up -d --build bff prometheus grafana`. If Prometheus was
already running, reload its scrape configuration with
`docker compose restart prometheus`. Confirm that `frame-inventory-bff` is
**UP** in [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets). Prometheus scrapes
`http://bff:9465/metrics` on the Compose network.

Open [Frame Inventory BFF](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-bff/frame-inventory-bff)
for GraphQL request rate, error percentage, p50/p95/p99 latency, in-flight
requests, and event loop utilization. The **Slowest queries and mutations (p95)**
panel ranks top-level fields such as `frames` and `updateFrame` by resolver
latency over the selected time range. Run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md)
several times across at least two scrapes. Run `{ frames(page: -1) { page } }`
to generate a GraphQL error. The dashboard counts GraphQL errors even when
Apollo responds with HTTP 200.

### Backend and BFF logs

Run `docker compose up -d --build bff grafana`. Alloy reads the backend and
BFF containers’ stdout and stderr through the Docker socket and sends them
to Loki. Loki stores logs in the `loki-data` volume with seven-day retention.
For a failed GraphQL request, take the `X-Correlation-Id` response header
and search both services with
`{service_name=~"backend|bff"} | json | correlationId="your-id"`.
For a production deployment, configure log storage, retention, and access
controls for that environment.

Open [Grafana Explore](http://127.0.0.1:3001/explore), select **Loki**,
and switch to **Code** mode to run either LogQL query.

- Backend — `{service_name="backend"}`
- BFF — `{service_name="bff"}`

### OpenTelemetry Collector

Run `docker compose up -d --build otel-collector` to start the Collector and its
dependencies. The Collector scrapes `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus`
every 15 seconds and exposes the latest samples on localhost. Once the backend
is ready and the first scrape completes, check for a JVM metric from Spring Boot.

```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:9464/metrics | rg '^jvm_memory_used_bytes\{'
```

## Running modules without Docker

### Backend

Start PostgreSQL before running the backend locally. Spring Boot applies the
Flyway migrations on startup.

```bash
docker compose up -d --wait postgres
cd src/backend
./gradlew bootRun
```

### Frontend

```bash
cd src/frontend
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Inventory import development services

Compose starts Temporal and the S3/SQS emulator. Set
`INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN` in the root `.env` to enable **Imports** and
follow the [browser verification steps](src/frontend/README.md#verify-a-delta-import-in-the-browser).
The [Temporal UI](http://127.0.0.1:8233) shows each import workflow.

See [inventory import infrastructure](infra/inventory-import/README.md) for
emulator configuration, Terraform, and the infrastructure smoke test.
# Inventory import infrastructure

This Terraform root provisions a dedicated versioned S3 bucket, a standard SQS
queue, and a dead-letter queue in one region. S3 sends PUT notifications for
`uploads/*/inventory_frame.csv` directly to the source queue. Attach the
output application policy to the backend's existing execution role. The
backend will use the bucket name and both queue URLs as import configuration.

## Local development

From the repository root:

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait aws temporal
```

Compose pins the LocalStack community image from before token activation
became mandatory. It exposes S3/SQS on `127.0.0.1:4566` and Temporal on
`127.0.0.1:7233` with UI on port 8233. Containers on the Compose network can
reach `aws:4566` and `temporal:7233`. Use the loopback S3 endpoint
with path-style addressing when signing URLs for a host browser. The ready hook
creates the bucket, queues and notification. The smoke test is intended to run
before starting a queue consumer.

```sh
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=REDACTED AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=REDACTED uv run infra/inventory-import/smoke.py \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4566 --region us-east-1 \
  --bucket frame-inventory-import-local --origin http://localhost:3000 \
  --queue-url http://127.0.0.1:4566/000000000000/inventory-import \
  --dlq-url http://127.0.0.1:4566/000000000000/inventory-import-dlq
```

## AWS sandbox

Use a dedicated sandbox account or a dedicated stack with idle queues. Configure
a remote state backend before sharing a deployment. An existing S3 state bucket
with locking enabled (`use_lockfile = true`) and a separate key for each
environment is suitable. Store state outside the import bucket. Supply
`aws_region`, `bucket_name`, `name_prefix` and `frontend_origins` with a local
`.tfvars` file or `TF_VAR_*` environment variables.

From this directory, initialize state and review a plan with sandbox
credentials:

```sh
terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=$STATE_BUCKET" \
  -backend-config="key=inventory-import/sandbox.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=$STATE_REGION" \
  -backend-config="use_lockfile=true"
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=sandbox.tfplan
```

Apply the reviewed plan in the sandbox. AWS recommends allowing up to 15
minutes for first-time S3 versioning to propagate before writing objects.
For static validation without AWS credentials, use
`terraform init -backend=false` followed by `terraform validate`.

Run the same smoke script with sandbox credentials for the application role,
the configured region and frontend origin, and the Terraform bucket and queue
outputs. Omit `--endpoint`. It checks browser CORS headers, a signed create-only
PUT and rejected replay, version-pinned reads, version-bearing notifications,
and DLQ redrive. The script creates one unique test object and deletes only the
matched event from the DLQ. Leave the test object to the lifecycle policy.

S3 makes live upload objects eligible for expiration after seven days. On a
versioned bucket this creates a delete marker. The underlying noncurrent
version is eligible for permanent expiration after one additional day. Cleanup
is asynchronous. Keep workflow and dispatch retries within the seven-day
window. The standard queue retains messages for four days and the DLQ retains
them for up to fourteen days from the original enqueue time.

{"id":"GLO-62","uuid":"3d144294-aff5-4cdb-9ce6-724c9ae6a75a","title":"Make CSV imports work with a single `docker compose up`","description":"CSV upload is a required feature, but out of the box it doesn't work:

* With no `.env`, `INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN` is empty. The `local-import` profile stays off, the BFF gets no import endpoint, and the Imports page can't create jobs.
* Copying `.env.example` to `.env` as it stands (`INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN=REDACTED stops the backend starting, because `LocalImportIdentity` requires a 64-character lowercase hex token.
* Even when it's set up, the user has to paste the token into the browser by hand.

A reviewer following the README hits one of these straight away.

## Proposed change

* Leave the token empty in `.env.example` (and the Sentry DSNs too) and add a comment: `# Generate with: openssl rand -hex 32`.
* Add a `just up` step, or a small script, that generates the token into `.env` if it's missing before running `docker compose up --build`.
* Document the steps in the root README under the smoke test, including where to paste the token in the UI.
* Optional: in the local profile only, have the frontend get the token itself, e.g. from a dev-only setting, so nobody has to paste it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a fresh clone, `cp .env.example .env && docker compose up --build` starts every service, including the backend.
- [ ] Following the README, a reviewer can upload `data/inventory_frame.csv` and see the job complete in the UI without generating a token by hand.
- [ ] An empty or missing token disables imports cleanly and the UI says why, instead of the backend failing to start.
- [ ] Startup rejects an invalid non-empty token with a clear error message that says how to generate one.

## Notes

* The token check is in `src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/inventoryimport/LocalImportIdentity.java`.
* The settings that switch on with the token are in `docker-compose.yml`: `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` and `IMPORT_GRPC_ENDPOINT`.

# This compose file is a starting point, not a requirement. You are free to

services:
  backend:
    build:
      context: ./src/backend
    container_name: frame-inventory-backend
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4000:4000"
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
      - "127.0.0.1:9090:9090"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:+,local-import}
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/frames
      SPRING_FLYWAY_ENABLED: "true"
      MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE: health,info,prometheus
      SENTRY_DSN: ${SENTRY_DSN:-}
      SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: ${SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT:-local}
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN: ${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:-}
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_BUCKET: frame-inventory-import-local
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_REGION: us-east-1
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_SIGNING_ENDPOINT: http://127.0.0.1:4566
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_ENABLED: "true"
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_AWS_ENDPOINT: http://aws:4566
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_QUEUE_URL: http://aws:4566/000000000000/inventory-import
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_DLQ_URL: http://aws:4566/000000000000/inventory-import-dlq
      INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_TARGET: temporal:7233
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: test
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: test
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      aws:
        condition: service_healthy
      temporal:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator/health"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      frame-inventory:
        aliases: [bff]

  bff:
    build:
      context: ./src
      dockerfile: bff/Dockerfile
    # Keep the import gRPC connection on loopback.
    network_mode: service:backend
    environment:
      FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT: ${FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT:-127.0.0.1:9090}
      IMPORT_GRPC_ENDPOINT: ${INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN:+127.0.0.1:9090}
      BFF_LISTEN_HOST: 0.0.0.0
      OTEL_EXPORTER_PROMETHEUS_HOST: 0.0.0.0
      SENTRY_DSN: ${BFF_SENTRY_DSN:-}
      SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: ${SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT:-local}
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy

  frontend:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: src/frontend/Dockerfile
    container_name: frame-inventory-frontend
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    environment:
      BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8080
      BFF_URL: http://bff:4000
    volumes:
      - ./src/frontend/src:/app/src/frontend/src
      - ./src/frontend/public:/app/src/frontend/public
      - ./src/frontend/next.config.ts:/app/src/frontend/next.config.ts:ro
      - ./design-system:/app/design-system:ro
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - bff
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

      SQS_ENDPOINT_STRATEGY: dynamic
      S3_SKIP_SIGNATURE_VALIDATION: "0"
    volumes:
      - ./infra/inventory-import/local/init-aws.sh:/etc/localstack/init/ready.d/init-aws.sh:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "test", "-f", "/tmp/inventory-import-ready"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  temporal:
    image: temporalio/temporal:1.5.1
    command: ["server", "start-dev", "--ip", "0.0.0.0"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:7233:7233"
      - "127.0.0.1:8233:8233"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "temporal", "operator", "cluster", "health", "--address", "127.0.0.1:7233"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  workflows:
    build:
      context: ./src

      - backend
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

    image: grafana/loki:3.7.0

      - frame-inventory

  alloy:
    image: grafana/alloy:v1.21.0

    depends_on:

# Frame Inventory

Application for the frame-inventory take-home exercise.

## System Overview

Next.js serves the inventory and import workspace. It sends GraphQL requests through a same-origin route to the BFF, which calls Spring Boot over gRPC. Docker Compose runs these services alongside PostgreSQL, Temporal, a local S3/SQS emulator, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and the OpenTelemetry Collector. The exercise provides a legacy export in `data/inventory_frame.csv` and describes the inventory features in `INSTRUCTIONS.md`.

Bring the whole stack up with one command.

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

Once PostgreSQL is healthy, the backend applies pending Flyway migrations during startup.

If you have `just` installed, run `just` to list the available recipes.

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `just up` | Build and start the whole stack in the foreground. |
| `just down` | Stop the stack and retain its named data volumes. |
| `just compose logs -f backend` | Pass arguments through to Docker Compose. |
| `just migrate` | Run Flyway on its own in a one-off backend container. |

## Subdirectories & System Boundaries

- [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the Spring Boot backend, Apollo Server BFF, and Next.js frontend.
- [Design system](./design-system/README.md) contains the prototype, sample frame data, and visual conventions for the exercise.

## Services

`docker compose up` starts the following services.

| Service               | Host port | Container port | Notes                                                  |
|-----------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| frontend              | 3000      | 3000           | Next.js workspace and same-origin GraphQL route     |
| bff                   | 4000      | 4000           | Apollo Sandbox and the frame inventory GraphQL API     |
| backend               | 8080      | 8080           | Spring Boot, exposes `GET /api/health`                 |
| postgres              | 5432      | 5432           | Spring Boot applies the inventory schema via Flyway    |
| aws                   | 4566      | 4566           | Local S3 and SQS for CSV imports                      |
| temporal              | 7233, 8233 | 7233, 8233    | Temporal gRPC and web UI                              |
| workflows             |           |              | Python Temporal worker for DELTA imports              |
| prometheus            | 9091      | 9090           | Scrapes Spring Boot and Apollo metrics every 15 seconds |
| otel-collector        | 9464      | 9464           | Scrapes Spring Boot metrics for local inspection       |
| grafana               | 3001      | 3000           | Queries provisioned Prometheus and Loki data            |

### Credentials

| Service               | User       | Password       | Database         |
|-----------------------|------------|----------------|------------------|
| postgres              | `app`      | `app`          | `frames`         |
| grafana               | `admin`    | `admin`         | n/a              |

## Global Invariants

- The Next.js rewrite preserves the `/api/` path and uses `BACKEND_URL` as its destination origin. Compose sets it to `http://backend:8080`. `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.frontend.environment.BACKEND_URL]`
- The Next.js `/api/graphql` route proxies GraphQL to `BFF_URL`. Compose sets it to `http://bff:4000`.

## Global Side Effects

- Opening the frontend loads the first page of frames. Starting an import uploads the file directly to S3 using the signed URL returned by the BFF.
- Docker Compose publishes service ports and creates named volumes for PostgreSQL, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and Alloy. `[docker-compose.yml:services]` `[docker-compose.yml:volumes]`

## System Verification

- From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test`.
- From `src/frontend`, run `npm run lint` after installing dependencies.

### Git hooks

Install [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/#installation), then run `pre-commit install`
from the repository root to install both Git hooks. The `pre-commit` hook checks
YAML, JSON, and merge conflict markers, and runs ESLint when staged changes touch
`src/frontend/`. Install the frontend dependencies with `npm ci --prefix src/frontend`
before committing frontend changes.

The `commit-msg` hook uses Commitlint to enforce the Conventional Commits format
documented in [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md). Commitlint requires Node.js 22.12 or newer.

Run `pre-commit run --all-files` to check the whole repository.

### Smoke test

Once the stack is up, check the service entry points.

- Open <http://localhost:3000> to view the frame list. See the [frontend setup](./src/frontend/README.md) to enable local imports.
- Hit the backend directly: <http://localhost:8080/api/health>.
- Open [Apollo Sandbox](http://127.0.0.1:4000) and run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md).

### Backend metrics

- Open [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets) and wait for the
  `frame-inventory-backend` target to show **UP**. It scrapes
  `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus` on the Compose network.
- Open [Grafana](http://127.0.0.1:3001), sign in with the initial credentials
  above, and run `up{job="frame-inventory-backend"}` in **Explore** using the
  default Prometheus data source. A value of `1` confirms the backend is being scraped.
- Open [Frame Inventory Backend](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-backend/frame-inventory-backend)
  for HTTP and gRPC request rate, errors, p50, p95, and p99 latency, and resource saturation.
  Generate API traffic and allow at least two Prometheus scrapes for request graphs
  to populate.
- The **Frame inventory activity** section shows committed creates, updates, and
  soft deletes, plus successful gRPC reads and version conflicts. The totals cover
  the dashboard time range. Rejected or rolled-back writes and repeated deletes
  that change no data are excluded from the totals.

Prometheus and Grafana listen on localhost. Their named volumes keep metrics
and Grafana settings across restarts.

### DELTA import dashboard

The main Compose stack scrapes import metrics from the backend. For the
host-based [local import setup](src/backend/README.md#local-import-operator),
start Spring Boot with the dispatcher enabled and run the
[Python worker](src/workflows/README.md). Set
`MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE=health,info,prometheus` and keep HTTP
port 8080 reachable from Docker. On Docker Desktop, scrape that host backend
with the local import Compose override.

```sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f monitoring/compose.local-import.yml \
```

Open [Frame Inventory Imports](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-imports/frame-inventory-imports)
to see the oldest pending and running jobs, terminal dispatch failures in the
last hour, and mean and p95 apply duration. The age uses dispatch confirmation
when available and job creation otherwise. Apply duration covers each activity
attempt, including retries. Use the import job ID to find its

To return to scraping the containerized backend and BFF, run
`docker compose up -d prometheus grafana` with the standard Compose configuration.

Run `docker compose up -d --build bff prometheus grafana`. If Prometheus was

Run `docker compose up -d --build bff grafana`. Alloy reads the backend and

to Loki. Loki stores logs in the `loki-data` volume with seven-day retention.

and search both services with
`{service_name=~"backend|bff"} | json | correlationId="your-id"`.

controls for that environment.

Open [Grafana Explore](http://127.0.0.1:3001/explore), select **Loki**,

- Backend — `{service_name="backend"}`
- BFF — `{service_name="bff"}`

# Inventory import infrastructure

This Terraform root provisions a dedicated versioned S3 bucket, a standard SQS
queue, and a dead-letter queue in one region. S3 sends PUT notifications for
`uploads/*/inventory_frame.csv` directly to the source queue. Attach the
output application policy to the backend's existing execution role. The
backend will use the bucket name and both queue URLs as import configuration.

## Local development

From the repository root:

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait aws temporal
```

Compose pins the LocalStack community image from before token activation
became mandatory. It exposes S3/SQS on `127.0.0.1:4566` and Temporal on
`127.0.0.1:7233` with UI on port 8233. Containers on the Compose network can
reach `aws:4566` and `temporal:7233`. Use the loopback S3 endpoint
with path-style addressing when signing URLs for a host browser. The ready hook
creates the bucket, queues and notification. The smoke test is intended to run

```sh
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4566 --region us-east-1 \

```

## AWS sandbox

Use a dedicated sandbox account or a dedicated stack with idle queues. Configure
a remote state backend before sharing a deployment. An existing S3 state bucket
with locking enabled (`use_lockfile = true`) and a separate key for each
environment is suitable. Store state outside the import bucket. Supply
`aws_region`, `bucket_name`, `name_prefix` and `frontend_origins` with a local
`.tfvars` file or `TF_VAR_*` environment variables.

From this directory, initialize state and review a plan with sandbox
credentials:

```sh
terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=$STATE_BUCKET" \
  -backend-config="key=inventory-import/sandbox.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=$STATE_REGION" \
  -backend-config="use_lockfile=true"
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=sandbox.tfplan
```

Apply the reviewed plan in the sandbox. AWS recommends allowing up to 15
minutes for first-time S3 versioning to propagate before writing objects.
For static validation without AWS credentials, use
`terraform init -backend=false` followed by `terraform validate`.

Run the same smoke script with sandbox credentials for the application role,
the configured region and frontend origin, and the Terraform bucket and queue
outputs. Omit `--endpoint`. It checks browser CORS headers, a signed create-only
PUT and rejected replay, version-pinned reads, version-bearing notifications,
and DLQ redrive. The script creates one unique test object and deletes only the
matched event from the DLQ. Leave the test object to the lifecycle policy.

S3 makes live upload objects eligible for expiration after seven days. On a
versioned bucket this creates a delete marker. The underlying noncurrent
version is eligible for permanent expiration after one additional day. Cleanup
is asynchronous. Keep workflow and dispatch retries within the seven-day
window. The standard queue retains messages for four days and the DLQ retains
them for up to fourteen days from the original enqueue time.

# AGENTS.md

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Merge with project-specific instructions as needed.

Tradeoff: These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

1. Think Before Coding

Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.

Before implementing:

State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.

If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.

If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.

If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

2. Environment & Runtime

Ensure toolchain consistency before execution.

Always check for the presence of a .nvmrc file in the root directory.

Before installing dependencies, running scripts, or building the project, ensure the correct Node.js version is active in the current shell session:

export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"
[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"
nvm use


If nvm is not installed in the subshell, verify node -v matches .nvmrc before proceeding. If nvm use fails due to a missing local version, stop and log that nvm install is required.

3. Simplicity First

Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.

No features beyond what was asked.

No abstractions for single-use code.

No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.

No error handling for impossible scenarios.

If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

4. Surgical Changes

Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.

When editing existing code:

Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.

Don't refactor things that aren't broken.

Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.

If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.

Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

5. Goal-Driven Execution

Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

"Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"

"Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"

"Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]

[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

6. TypeScript Style Guide

Strict typing and modern TypeScript conventions.

Strict Typing: Adhere to strict: true compiler rules. Explicitly type all variables, parameters, and return types where inference isn't structural or explicitly clear.

Functions & Methods: All exported functions, component props, and helper functions must include explicit parameter types and a return type annotation. Inline array callbacks (e.g., .map(), .filter()) may rely on contextual inference.

Modern Syntax: Prefer modern ESNext and TypeScript features. Use standard utility types like Record<string, unknown>, and union types like string | null or string | undefined.

Specificity: Avoid using any. If a type is genuinely dynamic or unknown, use unknown and narrow it downstream using type guards or conditional blocks. Use is predicates for custom type guards.

Interfaces vs. Types: Use interface for structural object definitions that benefit from declaration merging or extensions, and type for aliases, unions, intersections, or primitives.

7. Next.js & React Conventions

Routing: Follow the repository's existing routing structure (App Router vs. Pages Router—see docs/architecture.md). Do not mix router paradigms.

Server vs. Client Boundaries: When using App Router, default to React Server Components (RSC). Add 'use client' only when React hooks, browser APIs, or interactive event handlers are required, keeping client boundaries as close to leaf components as possible. Never import server-only modules or secrets into client components.

Data Fetching & State: Follow the project's established Apollo data-fetching and caching patterns rather than introducing ad-hoc fetch calls or new state management libraries.

Navigation & Media: Prefer next/link (<Link>) for internal navigation and next/image (<Image>) for images unless existing patterns dictate otherwise.

Environment Variables: Never expose server-only secrets or private API keys with the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.

8. Commands & Verification

Check package.json for exact script names and use the repository's lockfile package manager (npm, pnpm, or yarn):

Typecheck: npm run typecheck (or npx tsc --noEmit)

Lint: npm run lint

Unit Tests (Jest): npm test -- <path-to-test>

E2E Tests (Cypress): npm run cypress:run

9. Testing

Unit test with Jest. Cover new features with e2e where feasible.

Write unit tests with Jest for new logic, components, and bug fixes.

Where a feature involves a user-facing flow, add or extend a Cypress e2e test (see cypress/) if feasible within the scope of the task.

Don't retrofit tests onto unrelated existing code - follow Section 4 (Surgical Changes).

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:

* State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
* If multiple interpretations exist, present them — don't pick silently.

* If something is unclear (e.g., `.proto` contract changes, transaction boundaries, or domain invariants), stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

* No abstractions or Strategy interfaces for single-use code (apply OCP when variation actually exists or is requested).
* No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
* No defensive `try-catch` blocks or error handling for impossible scenarios.
* If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:

* Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
* Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
* Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
* If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it — don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

* Remove imports, variables, fields, or private methods that YOUR changes made unused.
* Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

* "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"

## 5. Tech Stack & Conventions

* **Language:** Java 21+ (Prefer `record` for immutable domain DTOs/commands, pattern matching, and modern standard library features).
* **Framework:** Spring Boot 3.4+ with **Spring gRPC** (`org.springframework.grpc:spring-grpc-spring-boot-starter`).
* **Serialization / RPC:** Protocol Buffers (`proto3`) & gRPC.

## 7. SOLID Principles in Spring Boot & gRPC

### S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

*A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.*

* **gRPC Adapters (`*ImplBase` subclasses) & Controllers:** Responsible *only* for handling transport concerns—unwrapping and validating incoming Protobuf messages (or HTTP requests), delegating to an application service/use case, mapping the domain result back to a Protobuf response, and completing the `StreamObserver` (`onNext()` / `onCompleted()`). Never put business logic or direct repository calls in a gRPC service implementation.
* **Services (`@Service`):** Contain pure business logic and transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`). Break down large "God Services" into smaller, cohesive, domain-focused services or use cases.
* **Repositories (`@Repository`):** Responsible *only* for data persistence and retrieval. Do not include business rules in custom queries or repository implementations.
* **Mappers:** Use dedicated mapper classes or MapStruct to convert between Protobuf messages, Domain models, and JPA Entities. Do not bloat entities, stubs, or services with mapping logic.

### O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

*Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.*

* **Strategy Pattern with Spring DI:** When multiple implementations or business rule variants exist (e.g., payment processing, notification channels, discount calculations), avoid large `if-else` or `switch` statements. Define a common interface and inject a `List<StrategyInterface>` or `Map<String, StrategyInterface>` via Spring's dependency injection to resolve implementations dynamically.
* **gRPC Interceptors (`ServerInterceptor`):** Handle cross-cutting transport concerns (authentication, logging, distributed tracing, and global exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` translation) via Spring-managed `ServerInterceptor` beans rather than repetitive `try-catch` blocks inside RPC methods.
* **Domain Events:** Use Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener` (or `@TransactionalEventListener`) to decouple side effects (e.g., sending an email after user registration) from core business flows.

### L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

*Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.*

* **Contract Adherence:** Implementations of an interface must honor the expected behavior, preconditions, and postconditions of the interface.
* **No Unsupported Operations:** Never implement an interface method by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. If a class cannot fulfill the entire interface contract, the interface is too broad (see ISP).
* **Exception Consistency:** Subclasses or interface implementations should not throw unexpected checked or runtime exceptions that violate the caller's expectations of the base type.

### I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

*Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.*

* **Focused `.proto` Contracts:** Keep gRPC service definitions granular and domain-aligned (e.g., `UserQueryService`, `UserCommandService`) rather than monolithic `.proto` files with dozens of unrelated RPCs.
* **Role-Specific Java Interfaces:** Avoid bloated Java interfaces. Split them into focused interfaces based on client needs (e.g., `UserQueryUseCase`, `UserRegistrationUseCase`).
* **Repository Interfaces:** Do not blindly extend `JpaRepository` if a consumer only needs read access. Consider defining custom base repository interfaces (e.g., `ReadOnlyRepository<T, ID>`) exposing only `findById` and `findAll`.

### D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.*

* **Strict Boundary Isolation (Protobuf & JPA):** Never leak generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) or JPA `@Entity` classes into the core `application` or `domain` layers. Map both Protobuf messages and JPA Entities to/from pure Java domain models (`record` or domain classes) at the outer adapter boundaries.
* **Depend on Abstractions:** Core domain/business services must depend on interfaces (ports) rather than concrete infrastructure classes (adapters) like external gRPC stubs (`*BlockingStub`), REST clients, or third-party SDKs.

## 8. gRPC & Protocol Buffers Guidelines

* **Contract-First Development:** Place all `.proto` definitions in `src/main/proto/` organized by domain and version (e.g., `src/main/proto/user/v1/user.proto`).
* **Proto Options:** Always include `option java_multiple_files = true;` and a clear `option java_package = "...";` so generated classes are clean and modular. Never manually modify generated Java stub files under `target/generated-sources/` or `build/generated/`.
* **Protobuf Defaults & Presence:** Remember that `proto3` scalar fields default to zero-values (`0`, `""`, `false`) and cannot be `null`. Use the `optional` keyword or wrapper types in `.proto` when distinguishing between unset and default values is required by business logic.
* **Error Mapping:** Throw domain-specific exceptions in the service layer (e.g., `ResourceNotFoundException`, `InvalidArgumentDomainException`) and translate them centrally into appropriate `io.grpc.Status` codes (`Status.NOT_FOUND`, `Status.INVALID_ARGUMENT`, etc.) at the gRPC interceptor/advice boundary.

## 9. Recommended Package Structure

Organize packages by **feature/domain** using Hexagonal / Clean Architecture boundaries so transport (gRPC/REST) and persistence remain completely decoupled from business logic:

```text
src/main
├── proto
│   └── feature/v1              # .proto contract definitions
└── java/com/example/project
    ├── common                  # Shared utilities, interceptors, base configs
    │   ├── grpc                # Global gRPC ServerInterceptors & Status exception mappers
    │   └── config              # Security, gRPC, and Jackson configurations
    └── feature                 # e.g., order, user, payment
        ├── adapter             # Inbound & Outbound Adapters
        │   ├── in.grpc         # gRPC *ImplBase services & Protobuf Mappers
        │   ├── in.web          # (Optional) @RestController & HTTP DTOs
        │   └── out.persistence # JPA Entities, Spring Data Repositories, Entity Mappers
        ├── application         # @Service classes, Use Case implementations, Event Listeners
        └── domain              # Pure Java Domain Models, Records, Ports (Interfaces), Domain Exceptions
```

## 10. Coding Standards & Transactions

* **Transactions:** Place `@Transactional` on application service methods that modify state. Use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query-only service methods to optimize database performance.
* **Validation:** Validate incoming Protobuf requests immediately at the gRPC adapter boundary (or via `protovalidate` / custom validators) before invoking domain use cases. Enforce business invariants inside domain models.
* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests requiring a real database.
* **Assertions:** Prefer **AssertJ** (`assertThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnNotFoundStatus_whenUserDoesNotExist() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        StatusRuntimeException ex = assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () ->
            stub.getUser(GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("missing").build())
        );

        assertThat(ex.getStatus().getCode()).isEqualTo(Status.Code.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

- This package is a standalone Apollo Server 5 service written in strict
  TypeScript. Use Node.js 22 and npm to match Docker and GitHub Actions.
- Apollo owns the GraphQL contract, pagination input validation, and translation
  of gRPC responses and errors. Keep inventory rules and persistence in Spring Boot.
- Use Apollo Sandbox directly at `http://127.0.0.1:4000/`. The Next.js application
  has its own entry point. See [README.md](./README.md) for a sample query.

## Schema and generated types

- Put GraphQL SDL in `schema/*.gql` and resolver implementations in
  `src/resolvers/`. `src/server.ts` loads the SDL with
  `@graphql-tools/load-files` and wires the resolvers into Apollo.
- Use the generated `Resolvers` type for resolver maps. GraphQL Codegen reads the
  same SDL as Apollo. `codegen.yml` maps GraphQL `Frame` to the generated gRPC
  output type.
- Use the [backend's frames.proto](../backend/src/main/proto/frameinventory/v1/frames.proto)
  as the Protobuf source of truth. Keep 64-bit version IDs as strings across
  the gRPC and GraphQL boundary.
- Regenerate files in `src/generated/` with `npm run generate`. The build also
  copies the canonical `frames.proto` to `dist/proto/frames.proto` for the
  runtime gRPC client.

## Validate resolver inputs

- Validate the allowed ranges and combinations of GraphQL arguments at the
  resolver boundary before making an upstream call. Keep these checks aligned
  with Spring's contract and preserve omission where Spring supplies a default.
- For each validation rule, test a valid boundary and a rejected value. Check
  that invalid input returns `BAD_USER_INPUT` and leaves the gRPC stub uncalled.
- The GraphQL `frames` query calls Spring's `ListFrames` RPC and returns
  `items`, `page`, `size`, and `hasNext`. Reject negative pages, sizes outside
  `1–50`, and null characters in `statuses` or `search` before calling gRPC.
  Treat omitted or null arguments as unset so Spring applies page `0`, size
  `25`, and no filters.
- The remaining operations are `frame`, `frameHistory`, `createFrame`,
  `updateFrame`, and `deleteFrame`. Pass expected version IDs to gRPC as
  positive 64-bit integer strings. An update replaces writable attributes.
- Throw `GraphQLError` with an `extensions.code` from `src/consts.ts`.
  The shared mapping in `src/frame-client.ts` uses `BAD_USER_INPUT` for
  `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `NOT_FOUND` for missing frames, `ALREADY_EXISTS` for
  reserved IDs, `CONFLICT` for gRPC `ABORTED`, `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` for
  `UNAVAILABLE` or `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` for
  unexpected failures.

## Logging and retries

- Cockatiel 3 supports the BFF's CommonJS build and Jest setup. Read-only RPCs
  retry only `UNAVAILABLE`, at most twice with 100 ms backoff. Every attempt
  shares the same five-second gRPC deadline. Send each mutation once.
- Use the shared Pino logger in `src/logger.ts` for structured service logs.
  Use `logger.info` for service lifecycle events such as startup. Use
  `logger.debug` for request-level diagnostics such as RPC duration or retry
  attempt number. Pino defaults to `info`. Set the logger level to `debug`
  when troubleshooting locally.
- Put diagnostic values in structured fields. Keep request payloads,
  credentials, and frame IDs out of logs. Log upstream status codes for service
  failures and keep client error messages generic for unexpected failures.
- Inspect Compose logs with `docker compose logs bff` from the repository root.

- From the repository root, start the Compose service with
  `docker compose up --build bff`. The multi-stage image builds the code and
